blocks.prompt: The Cave That a Raindrop Built
blocks.text: Rain falls on the hills. It soaks into the ground and finds a crack in the rock. The water is a little bit sour, like lemon juice but much weaker. Slowly, it eats the rock away. The crack turns into a hole. The hole turns into a room. After many thousands of years, there is a cave. Water still drips from the ceiling. Each drop leaves a speck of stone behind. Speck by speck, a stone icicle grows down. That is a stalactite. Under it, a bump grows up from the floor. That is a stalagmite. If they keep growing, they meet in the middle and make a stone pillar.

3.title: The Cave That a Raindrop Built
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

meta.templateLabel: The Cave That a Raindrop Built

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Caves are dissolved, not dug
Limestone is made of old sea shells
Stalactite has a c for ceiling
Stalagmite has a g for ground

blocks.prompt: Nobody Dug This Hole
blocks.text: Caves do not get dug. They get dissolved. It starts with rain. As a raindrop falls, it picks up a gas called carbon dioxide from the air. It picks up even more from the soil. That gas turns the water into a weak acid. It is far too weak to hurt you, but it is strong enough to bother limestone. Limestone is a soft rock made from the shells of sea creatures that died long ago. The sour water trickles into cracks. Every trip, it carries away a tiny bit of rock. One drop does nothing. A million years of drops carve out rooms, tunnels, and halls. Inside, the water keeps working. A drop hangs from the ceiling and leaves a ring of stone behind before it falls. Ring on ring, a stalactite grows down. The drop lands and leaves stone there too, so a stalagmite grows up. Here is how to remember them. Stalactite has a c for ceiling. Stalagmite has a g for ground. Neither one is in a hurry. Many grow less than the width of your fingernail in a hundred years.

4.title: The Cave That a Raindrop Built
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Cave That a Raindrop Built

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Rain plus carbon dioxide makes carbonic acid
Limestone is calcium carbonate
The drop leaves stone when its gas escapes
Caves have three zones: entrance, twilight, dark
The dark zone stays the same temperature all year
A stalactite and stalagmite that meet make a column

blocks.prompt: Why a Drop of Water Leaves Stone Behind
blocks.text: A cave is a hole that water thought about for a very long time. Rain begins the work. Falling through the air and soaking through soil, a raindrop absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes carbonic acid, a weak sour solution. Limestone cannot ignore it. Limestone is calcium carbonate, the pressed shells of ancient sea animals, and carbonic acid slowly dissolves it. The water finds a hairline crack, widens it to a finger, then to a fist, then to a passage you could walk down. The rock does not break. It leaves, one dissolved speck at a time, carried out in the stream. Then the water changes its mind. When a loaded drop finally hangs from a cave ceiling, it meets cave air, which holds far less carbon dioxide than the soil did. The gas escapes from the drop, the same way the fizz leaves an open soda. Without that gas, the water can no longer keep the limestone dissolved, so it sets down a ring of calcite before it falls. The next drop adds another ring. Over centuries the rings stack into a stalactite. Whatever the drop still carries, it delivers to the floor below, building a stalagmite upward. Give them long enough and they meet, and the cave grows a column. Caves are sorted into three zones. The entrance zone has light, wind, and ordinary plants. The twilight zone is dim, and the plants give up. The dark zone has never seen the sun, and its temperature barely moves all year, sitting close to the average yearly temperature outside. That steadiness is why bears once denned in caves, and why people sheltered in them. So the weather carved the cave, and then the weather decorated it.

(the limestone dissolves and is carried away in the water, speck by speck, rather than cracking off)
cave air holds less carbon dioxide, the gas escapes, and the water can no longer keep the limestone dissolved
(inference: a den that never freezes or bakes is a safe, steady place to sleep through winter)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Karst: a landscape dissolved by water
Speleothem: any cave formation
Mammoth Cave, Kentucky: 400+ miles mapped
Son Doong, Vietnam: has a jungle inside it
Troglobites live only in the dark zone
The olm is a blind salamander that may live 100 years

blocks.prompt: The Longest Dark
blocks.text: Nobody built the caves. Water dissolved them, and it took its time. The recipe is simple and slow. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and, more importantly, from the rich soil it soaks through. That gives it a mild acidity. Limestone, which is calcium carbonate laid down from the shells of sea creatures over millions of years, dissolves in mild acid. Groundwater follows the cracks and joints already in the rock and quietly widens them. A crack becomes a seam, a seam becomes a tube, a tube becomes a passage. Landscapes built this way are called karst, and they leak. Rivers vanish into the ground and reappear miles away. When the water table drops, the passage drains and fills with air. Only then does the decorating begin. A drop seeping into the empty chamber loses its carbon dioxide to the cave air, the same way a soda goes flat, and can no longer hold its dissolved limestone. It abandons a film of calcite on the ceiling and falls. Repeat for ten thousand years and you have a stalactite. Repeat below and you have a stalagmite. Cavers have names for the rest: soda straws, flowstone, cave popcorn, and draperies that ripple like curtains and glow when a light is held behind them. The whole family is called speleothems. The numbers are hard to hold in your head. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky has more than four hundred miles of mapped passage, and surveyors keep finding more. Son Doong in Vietnam is tall enough and wide enough to hold a skyscraper, and where its ceiling has collapsed, sunlight pours in and a jungle grows underground. Things live down there. Animals that spend their whole lives in the dark zone are called troglobites, and evolution has stripped them of what they cannot use. They tend to be pale, sometimes almost colorless, with skin grown over the place where eyes would be. The olm, a blind salamander in the caves of southeastern Europe, can go years between meals and may live a century. Losing your eyes sounds like a loss. In a place with no light, an eye is an expensive organ that earns nothing. A cave is not empty. It is the shape water left behind.

6.title: The Cave That a Raindrop Built
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Cave That a Raindrop Built

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Karst supplies drinking water to about a quarter of people
Degassing is why the drop leaves calcite
Stalagmites grow in yearly layers, like tree rings
Oxygen isotopes in calcite record past rainfall
Uranium in calcite lets scientists date the layers
Chauvet cave art is about 36,000 years old

blocks.prompt: The Cave as an Archive
blocks.text: Caves are among the few places on Earth where nothing happens quickly, and that turns out to be extraordinarily useful. Start with how they form. Limestone is calcium carbonate, the compacted remains of shells and coral pressed into rock over millions of years. It is nearly insoluble in pure water. But rain is not pure. A raindrop takes on carbon dioxide falling through the atmosphere, and takes on far more percolating through soil, where roots and microbes flood the pore spaces with the gas. The result is carbonic acid: weak enough to drink, and patient enough to hollow out a mountain. Groundwater follows fractures that are already there, dissolving the walls as it travels, converting hairline joints into passages wide enough to lose a person in. The surface above develops sinkholes, disappearing streams, and springs that surface miles from where the water went under. Geologists call the whole arrangement karst, and roughly a quarter of the world's people drink from it. Now notice the reversal. The same chemistry that excavates a cave is the chemistry that decorates it. Underground, saturated water seeps into an air filled chamber and immediately begins losing carbon dioxide to the cave atmosphere, which contains far less of it. This is degassing, the identical process that flattens an open soda. As the carbon dioxide leaves, the water's acidity falls, and it can no longer hold its dissolved load. Calcite precipitates. The drop leaves a microscopic ring on the ceiling and departs, the next drop leaves another, and after several thousand years there is a stalactite. The residue that survives the fall accumulates directly beneath it, and that is a stalagmite. Water is not building anything. It is simply failing to keep a promise it made in the soil. Here is where the patience pays off. A stalagmite grows in layers, adding a fraction of a millimeter each year for tens of thousands of years without interruption. Slice one open and the layers are visible, stacked like tree rings. Each layer is built from atoms delivered by rain that fell in a particular year, in a particular climate. Scientists read them. The ratio of oxygen isotopes locked in the calcite tracks the temperature and rainfall of the world above. Thick bands mean wet centuries. Thin or missing bands mean drought, and a stalagmite that stopped growing altogether is a drought long enough to be frightening. Because calcite traps trace uranium, which decays at a known rate, those layers can be dated precisely, which is more than can be said for most records of ancient climate. From a single column of rock in a dark room, a researcher can reconstruct hundreds of thousands of years of weather and check it against ice cores drilled on the far side of the planet. The archive is not only geological. The dark zone holds its temperature within a degree or two all year and keeps its humidity high, conditions that preserve almost anything left in them. That is why the oldest art our species has left behind is on cave walls. The paintings at Chauvet, in France, are roughly thirty six thousand years old. Lascaux, not far away, is about seventeen thousand. The horses and lions on those walls were drawn by people who had watched them closely, and they survive not because the artists chose their canvas well but because the cave refused to change. So a cave is a record kept by accident. Nobody meant to write it down. Weather dissolved the rock, weather decorated it, and weather signed its name in every layer. We are only now learning to read the handwriting.
